cards.front: Define a matrix and explain its dimensions using standard notation.
cards.back: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns. Its dimensions are denoted as $m \times n$, where $m$ is the number of rows and $n$ is the number of columns. An element at row $i$ and column $j$ is typically denoted as $a_{ij}$.

cards.front: State the necessary conditions for matrix multiplication $AB$ to be defined, and the dimensions of the resulting product $AB$.
cards.back: For the product $AB$ to be defined, the number of columns in matrix $A$ must be equal to the number of rows in matrix $B$. If $A$ is an $m \times p$ matrix and $B$ is a $p \times n$ matrix, then the resulting product $AB$ will be an $m \times n$ matrix.

cards.front: Calculate the matrix product $AB$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$.
Define a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix using transpose notation.
cards.back: A square matrix $A$ is **symmetric** if $A^T = A$. This means $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i, j$. A square matrix $A$ is **skew-symmetric** if $A^T = -A$. This means $a_{ij} = -a_{ji}$ for all $i, j$, which implies that all diagonal elements $a_{ii}$ must be zero.

cards.front: Prove that for any square matrix $A$, the matrix $A + A^T$ is symmetric and $A - A^T$ is skew-symmetric.
cards.back:
To prove $A + A^T$ is symmetric, we check its transpose:
$$(A + A^T)^T = A^T + (A^T)^T = A^T + A = A + A^T$$ 
Since $(A + A^T)^T = A + A^T$, it is symmetric.

To prove $A - A^T$ is skew-symmetric, we check its transpose:
$$(A - A^T)^T = A^T - (A^T)^T = A^T - A = -(A - A^T)$$ 
Since $(A - A^T)^T = -(A - A^T)$, it is skew-symmetric.

cards.front: Is matrix multiplication generally commutative? Provide a counterexample or explain why.
cards.back:
No, matrix multiplication is generally **not commutative**. That is, $AB \neq BA$ in most cases.

Counterexample:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
$$AB = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
$$BA = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
Since $AB \neq BA$, matrix multiplication is not commutative.

cards.front: Define the $n \times n$ identity matrix $I_n$ and state its unique property in matrix multiplication.
cards.back:
The $n \times n$ identity matrix, denoted $I_n$, is a square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. For any $m \times n$ matrix $A$, $A I_n = A$. For any $n \times p$ matrix $B$, $I_n B = B$. It acts as the multiplicative identity in matrix algebra.
Example $I_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

cards.front: Define the trace of a square matrix $A$ and state one of its key properties.
cards.back:
The trace of a square matrix $A$, denoted $\text{tr}(A)$, is the sum of the elements on its main diagonal. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then $\text{tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii}$.

One key property is that for any two matrices $A$ and $B$ for which both $AB$ and $BA$ are defined, $\text{tr}(AB) = \text{tr}(BA)$, even if $AB \neq BA$. Other properties include $\text{tr}(A+B) = \text{tr}(A) + \text{tr}(B)$ and $\text{tr}(cA) = c \cdot \text{tr}(A)$.
